stories.title: Gen Z’s squeeze needs new words, and a lot more talk
points: From France and Belgium to Ireland and Spain, young Europeans are protesting over failing schools, college costs and rents; nearly 590 French high schools were affected, and over half of young Spanish adults still live with their parents.
A Mumbai psychotherapist sees conversation fading at home and work; a 2026 study finds daily spoken words fell by about 338 a year, from around 16,000 in 2005 to 12,700 by 2019.
Humanities professor David Lloyd Dusenbury notes that young, highly educated Gen Zers widely blame ‘capitalism’, a 19th-century word, for their dimmer prospects, and says new terms are overdue.
stories.why: Elders should guide Gen Z at work and at home, by talking, not just texting. With AI reshaping jobs, that guidance matters more than ever.
stories.other: The protests are about rent, fees and underfunded schools, and governments face real budget limits. Gen Z may want policy fixes, not advice from elders.

stories.title: How BorderPlus is turning India’s talent surplus into a global workforce
points: Founded in 2025 by upGrad co-founder Mayank Kumar and Ayush Mathur, it trains nurses, matches them with overseas employers and handles visas, documentation and relocation.
Germany is 90–95% of the business today; it is expanding into Japan and the Gulf, then plans English-speaking markets such as the US, UK, Australia and Canada.
Employers pay about €8,000–12,000 per placement; candidates pay ₹10,000 for the first month and ₹1.9 lakh after screening. It raised $7 Mn last year.
stories.why: Ageing nations need workers and India has them. Done well, a talent surplus becomes careers abroad.
stories.other: Germany is 90–95% of the business, hiring cycles can run 15 months, and visa rules and attitudes to migrant workers can shift. A global platform, or a German nursing pipeline?

stories.title: RBI chief: a failed India–US trade deal would do ‘some’ damage
points: Sanjay Malhotra says the impact depends on how far tariffs go, so it is ‘premature’ to put a number on it.
Deals with the UK and New Zealand are signed; around 10 more are under discussion, including Peru, Chile, Israel, Canada and the Eurasian Economic Union.
USTR Jamieson Greer said on 1 Oct a deal was not imminent; on 5 Oct Nirmala Sitharaman said talks had ‘reached a plateau’.
stories.why: Spreading trade bets beyond the US is India’s hedge.
stories.other: Can a string of smaller deals really make up for the US market?

stories.title: Acemoglu: AI will replace only about 5% of human work in 10 years
points: The Nobel economist says AI should be built to make workers better at their jobs, not to replace them, and that such ‘pro-worker AI’ is within reach of today’s models.
He expects only about 5% of what humans do to be replaced within 10 years and roughly 1.5% added to GDP, likening AI to electricity, which took decades to spread.
The US taxes labour at over 25% and capital near zero, which he says subsidises automation; the seven largest tech firms make up 60% of the NASDAQ.
stories.why: It tempers both job panic and AI hype, and says the direction AI takes is still a choice.
stories.other: He calls the 5% a guesstimate made two years ago, and admits models have advanced faster than he expected. Will the forecast hold?

stories.title: AI agents find two room-temperature magnet candidates for future memory
points: A team of AI agents designed a new compound and spotted a 1999 one as magnets with zero net magnetism that still sort electrons by spin.
The 1999 compound, KV[Cr(CN)₆], stayed magnetically ordered up to 376 K (103 °C); the new design may be hard to make in its useful form.
Band gaps and spin sorting are predicted by simulation, not yet measured; the code and calculations are public.
stories.why: It points to denser, faster computer memory, found partly by AI.
stories.other: Spin sorting is predicted, not yet measured; the real test is remaking the material in a lab.

stories.title: AI agents could cost US banks $500bn by winning savers better rates
points: AI assistants could flag better deals or sweep idle cash into money-market funds paying more than near-zero instant-access rates.
JPMorgan, Bank of America and Wells Fargo hold $1.6tn of non-interest-bearing deposits; paying 3% on them would cost $47bn a year, almost half their annual earnings.
Banks gain too: Bank of America says $400mn spent on AI brought $800mn of benefits.
stories.why: Your idle balance is your bank’s profit; an AI agent could change who keeps it.
stories.other: Will savers hand their money to a bot, and who is liable if it sends funds to the wrong place?

stories.title: Tim Harford: how AI tempts the lazy mind
points: The real risk, he argues, is not that we trust AI completely, but that we stop caring enough to check its answers.
Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark misremembered CS Lewis on stage, and Google’s AI misattributed a Lewis quote too.
Like the telephone, AI cuts both ways: it can spark deeper research or replace it.
stories.why: Having an answer isn’t the same as finding the truth.
stories.other: Shortcuts also free time for deeper thinking; the choice of how to use them is ours.

stories.title: Bjorn Lomborg: most recycling is a waste
points: Metals and some plastics are worth separating; much paper, glass and plastic costs more to collect and process than it is worth.
A Danish plan would cost nearly €4,000 per ton of CO₂ avoided, almost 50 times the European carbon price.
Japanese data put the socially optimal recycling rate around 10%; sorting takes households 26–29 minutes a week per person.
stories.why: Good intentions still need a cost check.
stories.other: Cost tallies can undervalue harm from landfill and litter. Do his sums count it fully?
